title: Make sense of audit events
description: Find the right activity, read the evidence and understand the organisation-wide audit boundary.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional administrator checking why a warehouse camera's settings changed. There may be plenty of activity in Hub. How do we avoid searching for a needle in every haystack?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Start with a date range and a specific question. Audit events record security, configuration and data operations in the current organisation. Combine the time window with the actor, action, resource or outcome to narrow the feed.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So an actor could be the colleague who made a change?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It could, but automated activity can identify a service instead. Keep the question precise: what happened, to which resource, and did it succeed? Refresh preserves your filters, while Clear removes them when you need to broaden the search.

chapters.title: Read the evidence behind the row

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: We find a likely row. Is its short table label the whole story?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Expand its details to inspect the evidence available for that action. It may include a permission decision, request context, affected identifiers or field changes. The exact metadata depends on the event.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Should every background event contain a browser address or user agent?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not necessarily. A background service doesn't have the same browser context as a person making a request. Missing browser evidence isn't, by itself, proof that an event is wrong. Read the operation and its context together.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The results span several pages. Does the browser download the organisation's entire history first?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Filtering and pagination happen on the server. Use the visible range, total and page controls to work through the matching events. Narrowing the filters is usually more useful than just asking for more rows.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And an empty result doesn't automatically mean nobody touched the camera?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. Check the organisation, dates and active filters. The troubleshooting notes also explain that routine activity isn't necessarily recorded as a user-intent event. Interpret the feed according to its documented coverage.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Who can inspect the organisation-wide feed, and can they tidy up inconvenient entries?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The page is for organisation owners and administrators. It provides no edit or delete actions. Other people can generate audit events through normal activity without gaining permission to inspect everyone else's history.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the safe habit to take away?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Ask a focused question, inspect the event details and respect the organisation boundary. Sensitive credentials aren't intended as audit metadata. Don't paste secrets into a search or a report just to make an investigation easier.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
